Ryan Davidson - Commissioner Rod Beck - Chairman Tom Dayley - Commissioner ADA COUNTY’S STRETCH OF BOISE RIVER GREENBELT THROUGH EXPO IDAHO REOPENS This stretch of greenbelt pathway that goes through Ada County’s Expo Idaho property is now reopened. # Page 3^page=3
3 ADA COUNTY ELECTED OFFICIALS, DEPARTMENT HEADS MEET WITH STATE LEGISLATIVE LEADERSHIP Annual Meeting allows County leaders to share issues of concern with Idaho Lawmakers By the time you read this, the Idaho Legislature will be days away from beginning its 2026 session. The new legislative session is an important time for counties in Idaho as well. In Idaho, the legislature largely determines what programs and services counties throughout the state must provide. State mandates drive most of what counties do. In early December key Idaho Legislators met with the Ada County Commissioners to discuss emerging issues that the board believes need legislative attention. Those issues include aligning county procurement rules with state rules and adjusting reimbursement rates that the state of Idaho pays to the county for housing state inmates in county jails. The most unusual topic discussed at the December meeting involved the rat infestation that started in Eagle last year and is now spreading. These breeds of rats are not native to Idaho, so there are no mechanisms in place to control them as pests or invasive species. Keep an eye out for legislation next year that could address this issue. Thank you to the lawmakers who attended the luncheon as well as county elected officials, and department heads who made themselves available to answer questions and provide details. This annual meeting underscores the collaborative relationship Ada County has with state lawmakers.

# Page 4^page=4
4 Collaboration is the foundation of every successful organization. Whether it’s the private or public sector, when people work together, good things happen. Ada County is proud to have been recognized for this kind of work ethic by the Community Planning Association of Southwest Idaho (COMPASS). Ada County Parks & Waterways, along with the Ada County Highway District (ACHD) and the Idaho Transportation Department (ITD), were presented with the Leadership in Collaboration Award by the Community Planning Association of Southwest Idaho (COMPASS) at the annual Board of Directors’ meeting. When the Eckert Road Bridge COMPASS “Leadership In Collaboration” AWARD in southeast Boise was closed in January 2025 due to structural damage, the emergency closure could have lasted for several years. However, the Idaho Transportation Department (ITD) promptly offered assistance with mitigation measures, allowing the current bridge to reopen until it can be replaced with a new structure in the future. ACHD, in partnership with ITD and assistance from Ada County Parks & Waterways, repaired all eight wooden piers and reopened the bridge on March 10, 2025 – just 39 days after closure and three days before Boise River flows increased from 300 cubic feet per second to 1,000. The quick work and exemplary collaboration among leadership and staff at all three agencies ensured that the major emergency repairs were accomplished quickly and efficiently, showcasing the power of collaboration. Pictured L-R: Michael Johnson, ITD State Bridge Engineer; Scott Koberg, Ada County Parks & Waterways Director; Dave Kuisti, ITD; Todd Burlile, ACHD; Craig Raborn, COMPASS and former Nampa Mayor Debbie Kling Pictured L-R: Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson; Ada County Parks & Waterways Director Scott Koberg; Ada County Commission Board Chairman Rod Beck; Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley

# Page 5^page=5
5 Eckert Road Bridge in Southeast Boise February 2025 ADA COUNTY COMMISSION CHAIRMAN ROD BECK NAMED AS NEW COMPASS BOARD CHAIRMAN The COMPASS Board is a regional body of local officials that plans for future growth, particularly transportation and land use in Ada and Canyon Counties, by setting priorities for spending federal funds, developing long-range plans like Communities in Motion 2050, and representing regional interests to state and federal bodies. Essentially, it ensures local governments collaborate on big-picture infrastructure and quality-of-life issues, impacting daily commutes, development, and the overall regional economy.

# Page 6^page=6
6 ADA COUNTY VICTIM SERVICES CENTER WELCOMES NEW PARTNER For 20 years this one-stop location has helped tens of thousands of individuals when they need it most The Ada County Board of Commissioners has signed a contract with the Trauma Intervention Program of the Treasure Valley (TIPs) to join our more than sixteen specialized partners at the Ada County Victim Services Center (ACVSC). The ACVSC provides essential services to anyone experiencing domestic violence, sexual assault, child abuse, elder abuse, stalking and or human trafficking. Individuals and families may receive assistance 24/7 in one central location. The Center has been an important part of our community since 2006. Anyone who needs our services can come through one door and have access to a multitude of specialized teams. For almost twenty years the ACVSC has provided wrap- around services to stabilize and support victims of violence. “The Ada County Victim Services Center is one of the most important resources we have in our community,” said Ada County Commission Board Chairman Rod Beck. “Whether an individual is walking in the door by themselves or if law enforcement brings them to our downtown location for assistance, this Center is a safe place where families and individuals can navigate through one of the toughest times in their lives.” “We are so proud to have the Trauma Interventions Program of the Treasure Valley join our list of highly skilled partners who are changing lives every day,” said Trina Allen, Ada County Victim Services Center Director. “TIP is comprised of specially trained and screened volunteers who are available 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. They are a perfect fit to join our other partners at the center.” Our list of partners includes St. Luke’s, St. Alphonsus, Ada County Paramedics, the Ada County Sheriff’s Office (including Kuna, Eagle, and Star), Garden City, Boise and Meridian Police Departments, Women and Children’s Alliance and Terry Reilly Health Services, TANTA Inc., Idaho Network of Child Advocacy Centers, Idaho Department of Child and Family Services, Ada County Prosecutor’s Office. If you or someone you know is experiencing interpersonal violence, please contact the Ada County Victim Services Center https://adacounty.id.gov/victimservices/

ADA COUNTY CELEBRATES THE250TH ANNIVERSARYOF THE SIGNING OF THEDECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE July 4, 2026 is the 250 th Anniversary of the Signing of the Declaration of Independence. This was a transformative document that forever shaped the history of the United States of America. In honor of this momentous occasion Ada County is celebrating in a fun way. Our goal is to have at least 90% of county employees sign a pledge promising to read the Declaration of Independence. The six month celebration starting in January will culminate with a giant county employee group photo at The Park at Expo Idaho. We’ll keep you posted on how to get involved. The Ada County Courthouse will be lit up with red, white and blue lights through July 4 th Red, white and blue landscaping will be featured where possible around the courthouse. Each month the Ada County Newsletter will include an article: “What the Declaration of Independence Means to Me.” A traveling digital kiosk will spend several weeks at each county location/office. The kiosk allows county employees to sign a digital pledge to read the Declaration of Independence

8 WESTERN IDAHO FAIR ANNOUNCES EXPANDED SCHEDULE STARTING IN 2027 The Western Idaho Fair has been a cherished summer tradition in the Treasure Valley, opening on the third Friday of August and running for ten days. Each summer, families and visitors from across the region gather to enjoy the Fair’s entertainment, exhibits, competitions, and community traditions. To continue meeting the evolving needs of fairgoers and families, the Western Idaho Fair will transition to a longer date range beginning in 2027. This change is based on ongoing community feedback and is intended to create a more accessible and flexible Fair experience for the public. Importantly, this change does not affect the 2026 Western Idaho Fair. The 2026 Fair will take place as previously scheduled, from Friday, August 21 through Sunday, August 30. The transition will begin in 2027, when the Fair moves one week earlier on the calendar and introduces a new 3-weekend format. In 2028, the final transition will occur, with the Fair opening date moving to the first Friday of August. The first Friday of August will serve as the opening day of the Fair in the years to follow. The Fair will be closed on Mondays and Tuesdays starting in 2027 with the new format. Western Idaho Fair Dates • 2026: Friday, August 21 through Sunday, August 30 • 2027: Friday, August 13 through Sunday, August 29 • 2028: Friday, August 4 through Sunday, August 20 “We consistently hear from families who want the Fair to begin earlier in August, before the back-to-school rush begins,” said Western Idaho Fair Director Bob Batista. “Starting earlier and spreading the Fair across three weekends allows us to offer more opportunities for families to attend while still keeping the Fair experience they know and love.” ADA COUNTY GOVERNMENT In addition to elected offices, Ada County government includes twelve individual departments. Each department provides important services to our residents in Star, Eagle, Meridian, Boise, Garden City, Kuna, and Unincorporated Ada County. These services include law enforcement protection, emergency preparedness, election services, parks & waterways, indigent services, juvenile services, solid waste management, the Western Idaho Fair, Weed, Pest & Mosquito Abatement and more. Learn more about the services provided to you by Ada County - www.adacounty.id.gov/

9 LIVING ON THE LAND: MAKING THE MOST OF YOUR SMALL ACREAGE This 12-week course, offered through a collaboration between University of Idaho Extension and the Ada Soil and Water Conservation District, is designed for new small- acreage landowners and anyone dreaming of owning acreage someday. This unique series has been helping small-acreage owners in Idaho make the most of their properties for over 20 years. In these workshops, participants explore topics essential for successful and sustainable land stewardship, including water rights, soil fertility, water quality, pasture management, animal husbandry, and much more. When: Every Thursday evening beginning January 8, 2026 Where: University of Idaho, Ada Extension Office - 5880 N Glenwood St., Boise, ID 83714 Who: Anyone interested in small-acreage property management and land stewardship Cost: $225 - covers registration for two (2) to attend the entire 12-week course plus a course notebook with all resources, soil test, water test, and refreshments Register at: https://www.adaswcd.org/living-on-the-land EVERY THURSDAY from January 8, 2026 - March 26, 2026 6:00 - 8:30 PM University of Idaho Extension, Ada County 5880 N Glenwood Road, Boise COST: $225 covers two (2) participants, copies of all slides and additional resources, a water quality test, a soil test, and refreshments Life on a small acreage is not all great views and beautiful sunsets. Whether your goals are to raise a few animals, create a productive hobby farm or just sit back and appreciate the wide open spaces, land management issues can bring you back to reality in a hurry. This 12-week workshop series is designed to support new and future small acreage owners as they learn the fundamentals of successful land stewardship, including basic soil health principles, water rights and basic irrigation, pasture management, animal husbandry, garden planning, integrated pest management and more. # Page 10^page=10
10 CONGRATULATIONS TO GARY JOHNSON ON 20 YEARS OF SERVICE TO ADA COUNTY Gary is someone who knows the fairgrounds better than just about anyone. Gary’s connection to this place started long before he ever worked for the county. Growing up showing livestock on these very grounds, Gary has truly known the fairgrounds for most of his life. That early start must have made an impression, because he eventually came back, not just to visit, but to take care of this place in a way that only someone with genuine roots here could. Over the past two decades, Gary’s knowledge has become legendary. If you need to know a name, a number, a date, or where something is, whether it’s above ground or buried three feet under – Gary already knows. And if he doesn’t know, give him a minute. He will. We also can’t talk about Gary without mentioning his background as a dairy farmer; a career that made him tough, resourceful, and, yes, a little FRUGAL. And honestly, that frugality has saved us more times than we can count. Gary can stretch a budget, repurpose a part, or fix something that everyone else thought was unfixable. Gary has never quite been the 9-to-5 kind of guy; he’s more of a 5-to-9 kind of fella. The kind of employee who’s here early, stays late, and jumps in whenever something needs to be done. The Western Idaho Fair doesn’t run on a normal schedule, and neither does he. And as if his commitment here wasn’t enough, Gary has also served as the Vice President of Meridian Dairy Days since 1998, a role that speaks volumes about his dedication to agriculture, community, and tradition. His passion for supporting local events and the dairy industry has reached far beyond our fairgrounds. And perhaps one of Gary’s greatest strengths: he gets along with everyone… well, most of the time anyway. From staff to vendors to guests, Gary knows how to meet people where they are and get the job done with patience, humor, and a whole lot of practicality. For 20 years, Gary Johnson has been a steady hand, a walking encyclopedia of Expo Idaho, and someone we can all depend on. We are truly grateful for the hard work, memories, and heart he has put into this place. The staff at Expo Idaho congratulates Gary Johnson on 20 years of dedication — and for everything he does to keep the grounds running, year after year. # Page 11^page=11
11 IT IS OUR PRIVILEGE TO RECOGNIZE KELLY INGRAM FOR 20 YEARS OF EXCELLENT SERVICE AS AN ADA COUNTY EMPLOYEE! After spending more than five years in administrative and planning roles in California – and a brief time with the City of Boise – Kelly Ingram joined Ada County. It was the same year YouTube first hit the internet - in 2005. Her first position in was in the Development Services Department where she worked for 2 years as a Planning Technician. Then in 2007, the same year Apple issued its very first iPhone - Kelly was promoted to a Planner I role. Just 8 months later she was again promoted to a Planner II position. After managing countless planning projects and being responsible for handling several planned community applications during the extremely busy years leading up to the economic downturn in 2008, Kelly transitioned to take over street naming and addressing for Ada County. Her position and responsibilities were eventually transferred to the Ada County Assessor’s Office where Kelly continued to work as an Addressing Technician for 5 years. In 2014—the same year Apple unveiled its first Apple Watch—Kelly made her way back to Development Services, accepting a position as an Administrative Assistant. She was promoted to Office Administrator shortly thereafter, a role in which she served for 3 years. She then took on the Department’s first ever Project Manager role in 2018, with the newly formed Strategic Planning Division and was - and continues to be - instrumental in the development and successful implementation of the County’s Capital Investment Program. Following the dissolution of the Strategic Planning Division, Kelly took on the Department’s Administrative Coordinator Position, the role she currently fills. Kelly’s institutional knowledge and experience have provided an exceptional foundation to allow her to make significant improvements across many disciplines and areas in the Development Services Department. Her contributions to office culture and professionalism will continue to influence and benefit employees in Development Services for years to come. Thank you to Ada County Development Services Director Richard Beck for the creative timeline write up!
